raw_response.country: Multiple countries (23 urban case study areas across Ghana, Jordan, Yemen, India, Lebanon, Bolivia, Tanzania, Nigeria, Ecuador, Indonesia, Pakistan, Nepal, Angola, Mexico, and Kenya)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban and peri-urban household and community drinking and domestic water service access supplied via private tanker water markets (TWM) alongside public piped water networks across 23 urban centers.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the review examines urban water governance, formal and informal institutions, market vs. public utility provision, and regulation of tanker water markets. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it systematically examines rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access across the case studies: (1) utility/service ownership and regulatory structure (private market tanker provision vs. public piped network supply, categorizing institutional regimes into formal licensing and water-quality regulations, unregulated legal markets, illegal markets, and vendor association self-regulation/price-fixing), (2) enforcement of licensing, chlorination/quality standards, groundwater extraction rules, and prohibitions on informal/illegal operators (Section 4.5.5, Table A1), and (3) tariff and cost-recovery rules (marginal distance-based TWM pricing and full cost recovery vs. subsidized public network increasing block tariffs, connection fees, and informal-settlement legal status barriers to piped connections).
criterion_notes.c3: Systematic empirical synthesis of 80 peer-reviewed and supplementary empirical case-study publications covering 23 urban centers, with explicit search queries (Table 1), selection criteria, research workflow (Figure 2), and structured extraction variables (Table A1).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service-access outcomes across the 23 urban case study areas: spatial accessibility (on-premises delivery vs. unconnected fringe/informal areas), temporal availability (mitigating piped network intermittency and storage constraints), water quality/acceptability, volumetric prices relative to network tariffs (4x to 400x), household affordability (reported as an issue in 14 of 23 cities, including expenditure-to-income ratios and low per-capita consumption), and horizontal/vertical equity (poverty penalty and exclusion).
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (23 urban centers with >50,000 population or >250 people/km2 and urban/peri-urban households and water users within them), exposure (private tanker water market organization, pricing/tariff rules vs. subsidized public piped tariffs, and formal/informal licensing, quality regulation, and enforcement regimes), outcome (spatial accessibility, temporal availability, quality, affordability, and equity of water access), and study design (systematic review of empirical urban case studies) are all clearly identifiable. Note that per Criterion 6, extractable quantitative effect sizes are a meta-analysis synthesis gate, not a systematic-review inclusion gate.

evidence_quotes.quote: The available evidence suggests that TWM have two key functions in urban water systems: (1) They provide services at otherwise unavailable levels, particularly with respect to the temporal availability and spatial accessibility of the service, and (2) they extend access to areas without or with low-quality network supply, typically low-income communities on the fringe of cities.

Formal institutions and regulations for TWM, such as licensing requirements of providers or quality regulations, exist in seven out of 14 locations and are partially enforced. In all of the studied areas, however, there was evidence of informal or illegal operators working alongside these formal TWM.

The combination of heterogeneous access to cheaper (subsidized) piped water and marginal pricing in TWM results in allocation outcomes that are not coherent with existing notions of equitable access to water.
In this article, we systematically summarize existing empirical knowledge on TWM and assess to what extent normative claims about the impacts of TWM on sustainability goals are supported by evidence.
23 case study locations and 80 literature items, listed in Table 2, were considered in the analysis.

In Nsukka, Nigeria, for instance, where more than half of the population uses tanker water services, the average per capita water consumption ranged at 35 L/day, whereas 7% of monthly income was spent on average to obtain water [138].

raw_response.exposure: Private tanker water market (TWM) service provision, market pricing/cost-recovery rules versus subsidized public piped network tariffs (and connection fee/tenure barriers), and formal/informal regulatory, licensing, quality-standard, and enforcement regimes
raw_response.outcome: Multidimensional urban water service access outcomes: spatial accessibility, temporal availability/continuity, water quality and acceptability, relative price (ratio to piped network tariffs), household affordability, and horizontal/vertical equity (poverty penalty)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 23 urban case study areas (population >50,000 or density >250 people/km2) across Africa, Asia, and South America synthesized from 80 peer-reviewed and supplementary empirical studies covering urban/peri-urban households, informal settlements, and tanker water providers
raw_response.rationale: This English-language systematic review synthesizes 80 empirical studies across 23 urban centers in low- and middle-income countries to evaluate how private tanker water markets (TWM) affect household and urban water service access. It satisfies all inclusion criteria, including Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading: beyond service delivery characteristics, it systematically extracts and analyses legality, provider licensing and water-quality regulations, regulatory enforcement (Section 4.5.5; Table A1), vendor self-regulation/price-fixing, and market marginal cost-recovery pricing relative to subsidized public network tariffs, connection fees, and informal-settlement tenure barriers, linking these institutional and tariff mechanisms to spatial accessibility, temporal availability, water quality, affordability, and equity outcomes.
raw_response.study_design: Systematic review of empirical urban case studies
